Modest empirical improvements (1-2.8%) with some large standard deviations; most experiments on small/medium datasets with no ImageNet-scale validation from scratch

Additional computational cost of clustering and early training stages not fully accounted for; claimed efficiency gains partially offset by identification overhead

Limited exploration of design choices: only GLIDE tested; minimal ablation on clustering vs. other partitioning methods; guidance scale and other diffusion hyperparameters not justified

strengths: Addresses a practical problem: efficient synthetic data augmentation by targeting only hard examples, reducing generation time to 30-60% of full augmentation
Provides theoretical analysis on simplified 2-layer CNN with results on noise suppression (Theorem 4.1), generation vs. upsampling (Theorem 4.2), and convergence properties (Theorem 4.3)
Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet, fine-grained), architectures (ResNet, ViT, ConvNeXt, Swin), and optimizers showing consistent improvements
Achieves computational efficiency gains: 3.6-4.8x reduction in generation time while maintaining/improving performance
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation and extensive ablation studies on design choices
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theoretical analysis uses highly simplified two-layer CNN with unrealistic assumptions (P=2 patches, cubic activation σ(z)=z³, orthogonal features/noise) that don't apply to modern deep networks; applicability to ResNet/ViT entirely unclear

Core method for identifying slow-learnable examples is ad-hoc: k-means clustering on model outputs lacks principled justification, no formal connection to Definition 3.1, and Table 7 shows only modest improvements over simpler baselines (loss-based, misclassification)
Theorem 4.2's key condition E[l_γ(t)⟨w_j,γ⟩²∥γ∥²] < (k+1)E[l_ξ(t)⟨w_j,ξ⟩²∥ξ∥²] cannot be verified a priori in practice; unclear how practitioners ensure synthetic noise satisfies this requirement

Limited novelty: Targeting hard examples is classical in data augmentation; using real images to guide diffusion models is known (He et al. 2023); core contribution is the combination but the method (clustering) is not principled

Weak baselines: Primarily compares against no augmentation and upsampling; only one comparison to DiffuseMix; missing comparisons to other targeted augmentation, importance weighting, or hard example mining approaches
No statistical significance testing: Results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests across multiple runs; unclear if 1-2% improvements are statistically significant

Limited experimental scope: Only tested on relatively small datasets (CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet); no ImageNet-scale experiments; single domain (image classification); no discussion of failure modes or dataset characteristics where method benefits most

Hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary and potentially tuned to test set: different k values for different datasets (k=5 for CIFAR, k=4 for TinyImageNet, k=2 for transfer) without principled justification; multiple denoising steps (40, 50, 70, 80) without clear selection criteria

Unclear synthesis image quality: How is t* for denoising initialization chosen? What guarantees synthetic noise is 'small'? FID scores vary 9x across denoising steps (5.36 to 47.35 in Table 6); 'faithful image' claims not rigorously validated

Two-stage training requirement: Method needs initial training phase to identify examples, then generation, then retraining; total computational cost including these stages is not clearly accounted for; inelegant compared to end-to-end approaches

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: selective augmentation of slow-learnable samples outperforms full augmentation, providing an interesting and counterintuitive observation
Rigorous theoretical framework: Theorems 4.1-4.3 provide sound analysis connecting feature learning homogeneity, noise suppression, and convergence properties, with connection to SAM dynamics

Comprehensive experimental validation: extensive evaluation across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet, fine-grained tasks), architectures (ResNet, ViT, ConvNeXt, Swin), optimizers (SGD, SAM), with thorough ablations
Practical efficiency: reduces computational cost to 30-60% of full augmentation while improving performance, addressing real practical concerns of existing synthetic augmentation methods
Clear presentation: well-structured paper with clear motivation, well-explained theoretical framework, and effective figures (especially Figure 1)
Consistent improvements: demonstrates robustness with improvements of 0.4-2.8% across diverse settings, including achieving better SGD performance than SAM on some benchmarks
weaknesses: Substantial theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis for two-layer CNNs with orthogonal features and Gaussian noise patches; real image data much more complex with correlated multi-level features; controlled logit assumptions (Eq. 3) restrictive; transferability to deep networks not rigorously justified

Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is sample selection strategy, not generation mechanism; uses standard GLIDE with existing real-image guidance technique from prior work (He et al., 2023); selection via k-means clustering acknowledged as heuristic and 'not the main focus'

Weak justification for slow-learnable identification: k-means clustering on model outputs lacks principled theoretical grounding; Table 7 ablations show only marginal differences between selection strategies; 'early in training' timing is vague; sensitivity to clustering epoch unexplored

Modest empirical improvements with incomplete statistical characterization: gains range 0.4-2.8%, with CIFAR-10 showing only 0.37% improvement; most main results lack error bars/confidence intervals; claimed improvements may be within noise levels for well-studied benchmarks

Limited baseline comparisons: primary comparison is against weak upsampling baseline; only one recent method comparison (DiffuseMix); missing comparisons with DreamDA and other recent diversity-seeking augmentation approaches

Hyperparameter sensitivity not thoroughly explored: multiple dataset-dependent hyperparameters (k ∈ [4,5], varying denoising steps); clustering epoch definition vague; no systematic sensitivity analysis for new datasets

FID score disconnect poorly explained (Table 6): FID increases 5.07→47.35 while performance initially improves then degrades; raises questions about what actually makes synthetic images useful; limited analysis of distinguishing good vs. bad augmented samples
Narrow application scope: only image classification evaluated; applicability to detection, segmentation, or other domains unclear; generalization potential limited
Missing failure analysis and significance testing: no discussion of when method underperforms or when full augmentation would be preferable; lack of formal statistical testing for modest improvements

Reproducibility gaps: k-means implementation details underspecified (clusters, random seed); 'early in training' needs precise definition; unclear how many random seeds used; some algorithmic details in Algorithm 1 remain vague despite pseudocode

strengths: Clear practical motivation: Addresses computational inefficiency of diffusion-based augmentation by reducing augmentation from 10-30× to 30-40% while improving performance
Solid theoretical analysis: Theorems 4.1-4.3 rigorously analyze why targeted synthetic generation outperforms uniform upsampling by showing generation prevents replicated noise amplification
Well-motivated generation strategy: Using real images as diffusion guidance to generate 'faithful' synthetic data is clever and theoretically justified—hard to achieve with standard augmentations
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple datasets (CIFAR/ImageNet), architectures (ResNet/ViT/ConvNeXt/Swin), optimizers (SGD/SAM), with thorough ablations across all key hyperparameters

Consistent and broad improvements: Up to 2.8% gains across diverse settings with significant computational savings (0.3-0.4× generation time); extends to object detection and works with different diffusion models
Practical efficiency: Reduces generation time substantially while augmenting only 30-40% of data—directly addresses computational bottleneck in diffusion-based methods
weaknesses: Substantial theory-practice gap: Theory assumes simplified two-layer CNN with P=2 patches and cubic activation; proves convergence only for early training phase, but experiments run full 200 epochs on modern deep networks. Key approximations (l_i^(t) = l_i,ε^(t)) are informal

Slow-learnable identification is heuristic: Authors acknowledge this 'is not the main focus,' yet it's critical. K-means clustering appears arbitrary with minimal justification; Table 8 shows only 0.45% gap between best and worst selection methods, undermining importance claims

Unvalidated theoretical assumptions: Theorem 4.2's key condition on synthetic noise magnitude is never empirically verified. How do we ensure E[l_γ^(t)⟨w_j^(t),γ⟩²∥γ∥²] < (k+1)E[l_ξ^(t)⟨w_j^(t),ξ⟩²∥ξ∥²] holds in practice?

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: Different k values per dataset (5 for CIFAR, 4 for TinyImageNet) with no principled selection strategy. FID score poorly correlates with performance (Table 7), undermining 'faithful' claim and suggesting tuning is non-intuitive

Modest improvements in important settings: ImageNet 0.33% gain (69.28 vs 68.95 Top-1); transfer learning ~0.84% improvement; object detection 0.77%—raises statistical significance concerns despite error bars

Reproducibility and implementation concerns: Code not available ('available a' incomplete); clustering algorithm unspecified; multiple hyperparameters require dataset-specific tuning; ImageNet uses only 16 epochs with different infrastructure (FFCV), limiting comparability

Limited principled sample selection: No comparison with sophisticated coreset/uncertainty-based methods. Ablation (Table 8) shows high-loss and misclassification nearly as good as clustering but less justified theoretically

Incomplete experimental analysis: No wall-clock time breakdown for full pipeline (train→select→generate→retrain); no failure case analysis; FID-accuracy disconnect unexplained; some results lack error bars

strengths: Interesting core idea of targeted augmentation for slow-learnable examples, offering practical efficiency gains (0.3-0.4× generation time)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, architectures, and optimizers with consistent improvements (up to 2.8% on TinyImageNet)
Theoretical analysis spanning noise suppression (Theorem 4.1), generation vs. upsampling (Theorem 4.2), and convergence properties (Theorem 4.3)
Thorough ablation studies on selection strategies, denoising steps, and design choices
Demonstrated applicability beyond classification to object detection
weaknesses: Substantial theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis on simplified two-layer CNN with two features does not convincingly explain performance on real high-dimensional datasets with complex feature hierarchies

Limited and weak baseline comparisons: primary comparisons are with USEFUL (authors' own baseline); ImageNet experiments incomplete (16 epochs vs. standard 90-100) with marginal improvements within noise (69.28±0.06 vs. 68.95±0.04)
Heuristic slow-learnable identification (early-training loss) lacks principled justification; why is high loss the right proxy rather than visual properties or learned difficulty?
FID-performance mismatch (Table 7) undermines faithfulness claims: higher FID sometimes yields better accuracy, suggesting synthetic images may not be 'faithful' as claimed
Unverified theoretical conditions: Theorem 4.2's condition on synthetic noise E[l_γ(t)⟨w_j,γ⟩²||γ||²]<(k+1)E[l_ξ(t)⟨w_j,ξ⟩²||ξ||²] is never validated empirically
Significant hyperparameter sensitivity: dataset-specific k values (5 for CIFAR, 4 for TinyImageNet), varying denoising steps, requires tuning separation epoch and cluster count
Clustering-based selection shows sensitivity (Figure 10) and lacks robustness analysis for selection errors

strengths: Novel core insight: Counter-intuitive finding that augmenting only 30-40% of data via targeted selection outperforms full augmentation, with 3-5x reduction in generation time
Strong theoretical framework: Theorems 4.1-4.3 rigorously explain why synthetic generation outperforms upsampling through noise suppression and convergence analysis, though on simplified setting

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive experiments across CIFAR-10/100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet, and object detection; multiple architectures (ResNet, ViT, ConvNeXt, Swin); multiple optimizers (SGD, SAM); consistent improvements up to 2.8%
Excellent ablation studies: Systematic analysis of selection strategies, denoising steps, upsampling factors, clustering configurations; thoughtful comparisons with USEFUL and other baselines

Good generalization: Works with different diffusion models, compatible with other augmentation methods, extends beyond classification to detection, and generalizes to traditional augmentation (TrivialAugment)
Practical efficiency: Clear computational cost reduction compared to prior work (10-30x augmentation); valuable for practitioners
Clear presentation: Well-motivated introduction, good visualizations (Figures 1, 7), and clear algorithm description
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theory restricted to simplified two-layer CNN with artificial data distribution (two features + orthogonal noise); unclear how theoretical insights (noise suppression, feature homogeneity) directly explain 1-2% improvements on real datasets

Theory-to-practice assumptions not validated: Theorems assume small learning rate and ρ, controlled logits, and early training phase; experiments use various ρ values (0.1, 0.05, 0.001) without justifying 'smallness' or validating theoretical predictions empirically

Method complexity and hyperparameter sensitivity: Multiple hyperparameters (separation epoch t, upsampling factor k varies 2-5 across datasets, denoising steps 40-100, guidance scale) require tuning; limited guidance on selection; Table 6 shows 6% variance in CIFAR-100 with different k values

Incomplete selection strategy justification: Clustering approach used but Table 8 shows only marginal improvements over alternatives (4.42 vs 4.77 vs 4.87, no error bars); limited exploration of other selection methods; gap between theoretical 'slow-learnable features' and practical 'slow-learnable examples' unclear

Synthetic image generation approach lacks novelty: Method adds noise to real images then denoises (conditional editing) rather than pure generation; Table 7's finding that FID doesn't correlate with performance is counterintuitive and under-investigated—why worse FID sometimes yields better results?
Missing statistical rigor: Some improvements modest (1.63% on ImageNet ResNet18); error bars absent from Figures 2-3 (main results); no significance testing despite making performance claims

Limited comparative analysis: Only compared with USEFUL for selection methods; DiffuseMix and Boomerang comparisons limited (Tables 2, 9-10); systematic evaluation of TADA with other diffusion methods would strengthen paper

Incomplete computational cost analysis: Generation time reported but total training time including clustering not quantified; ImageNet uses FFCV (efficiency framework) making comparison with other works difficult; 16 epochs is very short—unclear if results hold for standard 100 epochs
Failure case analysis absent: No discussion of when TADA fails; unclear if certain image classes or dataset types are problematic; limited exploration of behavior on very small datasets
